content: Starting a channel for general discussion of logic development in cslib (hope that's appropriate).

My PR on natural deduction cslib#66 is finally ready for review, I refactored it significantly so that deduction trees are defined for minimal logic (which matches more nicely with computational applications), and derivability/equivalence are relative to a Theory (set of propositions), which will make a more general semantic completeness result easy, as well as letting us add intuitionistic & classical principles to the logic. Feedback appreciated!
If this is CSLib specific conversation, it should probably be moved to that channel. Also you can link you can link to PRs like this: cslib#66

Nice! I don't have a specific comment, but wanted to ask this about "Logic in CSLib " for a while already: do we have a plan for accommodating multiple (very many?) different logics (or different proof systems for the same logic) and how they relate? So for example will we later also have natural deduction for First-Order Logic and will that formally extend the Propositional system in some way?
Or suppose :innocent: I want to do a specific modal logic, do I roll my own Proposition type for modal formulas and Derivation from scratch each time or can I somehow extend the types for the propositional system?

I think this is known as the Expression_problem and maybe my question is just whether people have thought about how to "solve" it in Lean.
Yes, at least for me, the ideal vision for CSLib is exactly what you describe. However, as far as I know, there's no concrete roadmap for it just yet.

I think that would be ideal, yes, but my two cents is that I feel there is a non-trivial tradeoff between generality in this sort of way and how closely things stick to computer science.

For example, the Formalised Formal Logic people have done a very good job of being modular — as I understand it, something like "conjunction elimination" is a typeclass on a deduction system, so results about conjunction elimination are valid for any deduction system which has it as a rule — but they (predominantly) use a Hilbert-style calculus. I started here with natural deduction because of how closely it sticks to the lambda calculus, and so it felt appropriate for inclusion specifically in a computer science library, even if it isn't the right formalism to prove things in full mathematical generality.

All that being said, some machinery along the lines of, "I want to define a type of derivations which is NJ.Derivation + some extra rules" would be great, and I am very open to reworking my PR to include it if someone knows how!

Also, I just added a note about a small design question to my PR cslib#66 — whether derivations should be parametric in a theory, giving them two kinds of axiom rules. I'd love some feedback here or there! (ping @Fabrizio Montesi as it's probably you who will review it)

I much agree that there is a trade-off between generality and usability of the instances of the general thing (be it formula or derivation types). And typeclasses as used in FFL can get quite far. I also think it might make sense to wait until a bunch of different logics are in cslib and how they are used by other areas before trying to find a general definition of what "a logic" is. But maybe not wait too long until all hope of unifying things is gone :wink:

Related to this, @Ramy Shahin gave a talk about a possible approach to the expression problem in Lean at TYPES2025, see paper and video. I do not want to suggest to make cslib depend on this (still quite experimental) code, but for the long term future it might be a nice inspiration.

(Another reason for circling back now is that I think we've accumulated some relevant experience from other simpler parts in cslib.)

Great! I agree that there are a lot of non-obvious choices to be made, & I'm very open to discussion &/or reworking what I've got as we go along. Probably the reference which is closest to how I've presented it is Sørensen & Urzyczyn's lecture notes, but I don't know of anywhere doing it exactly like I have, mostly because the needs of formalisation are a bit orthogonal to the usual way we write about proof theory imo.

I'd say most of the things you mention fall under formalisation choices: I'll try to write some more clarifying documentation, but to answer the things you raise here:

  • I wanted to capture minimal logic (intuitionistic without efq) because that's the one with the most obvious / direct computational content — essentially it is STLC with sums and products.
  • Once you're in minimal logic, either you don't have falsum, or it behaves exactly like an atom (ie there are no rules for it), so it seemed reasonable to have it be optional for a given language of propositions. In the case that it is present, we have ⊥ = atom ⊥ definitionally, so it doesn't really add much overhead i think.
  • The use of Theory is a bit less obvious. Usually on pen-and-paper you switch between minimal / intuitionistic / classical by adding and removing rules — since we don't have an easy way (cf above discussion) to do this as is stands, the best solution seemed to be to formulate the extra deduction rules as implications, and allow appealing to them as axioms.
  • Another point in favour of Theory is it makes it easy to define "equivalence modulo some axioms", which is nice in itself and helps with developing semantics.

Oh I didn't realize you were working from that, it's just a few feet away on my bookshelf. This is jumping way ahead, but if SOL is on your radar for the future, I would love to be able to formalize Wadler's The Girard-Reynolds Isomorphism. IIRC those notes do not go into the detail of the each direction of transformations between System F and second order logic. It would be a fun milestone of the library to see that our lambda calculus and logic developments line up in this way.

@Thomas Waring in cslib#91, would it be fair to say that you've formalised 'derivations with assumptions' (the assumptions being the theory T in Theory.Derivation)?

I'm starting to think that the concepts in cslib#89 about theories could make more sense to talk about what theories a proof theory gives (in terms of sets of derivable propositions), rather than assuming them a-priori to facilitate definitions, but maybe I'm wrong. :-)

That's more-or-less right I think — I have split "assumptions", which go in the context Γ, from "axioms" in the theory T, but the two are equivalent. The result Theory.Derivable.collect_axs in cslib#93 says that if Γ ⊢[T] B (B is derivable with assumptions Γ in the theory T) then there is a context Δ such that (Γ ∪ Δ) ⊢[MPL] B (B is derivable in minimal logic, ie with no extra axioms) and Δ ⊆ T — basically derivability in a theory T is the same as derivability where you can add some assumptions from T.

The point of having theories (in the form I have it) is so that we can have minimal / classical / intuitionistic deductions in the same type — you just add eg DNE to the theory. It's also quite convenient for semantics: you get a docs#GeneralizedHeytingAlgebra of (equivalence classes of) propositions for each choice of theory, and it has a bottom element iff the theory is intuitionistic, it's a Boolean algebra iff the theory is classical, etc.

I also considered the idea of a theory as a set of derivable propositions. Somewhere in one of my branches I defined this as a "closure" on the theory T: the bigger theory containing everything derivable from the axioms in T. I'm open to changing the name if you want to reserve "theory" for this notion, but I'm pretty sure making the type of deductions parametric in a collection of axioms (ie the theories I have now) is the right way to go for natural deduction.

I was tempted to use a checkmark, but we already use that for well-formed.. :-)
Derivable essentially means 'valid'.

I'd be willing to shift to

  • Γ ⊢[T] A for a sequent, defined now as a triple "theory + context + conclusion", maybe calling it Theory.Sequent instead of the current Sequent Atom
  • inherit ⇓(Γ ⊢[T] A) for T.Derivation ⟨Γ, A⟩ from InferenceSystem
  • find some notation for Derivable (Γ ⊢[T] A) to replace the current Γ ⊢[T] A
  • add analogous versions for the empty context to replace Theory.PDerivable

how does that sound?

here's the aforementioned pudding (having git Issues so i'll just paste the relevant code here)

def Theory.equiv.bindOfEquivImage {T : Theory Atom'} {f f' : Atom → Proposition Atom'}
    (hf : ∀ x : Atom, T.equiv (f x) (f' x)) : (A : Proposition Atom) → T.equiv (A >>= f) (A >>= f')
  | atom x => hf x
  | Proposition.and A B => (bindOfEquivImage hf A).mapAnd (bindOfEquivImage hf B)
  | Proposition.or A B => (bindOfEquivImage hf A).mapOr (bindOfEquivImage hf B)
  | impl A B => (bindOfEquivImage hf A).mapImpl (bindOfEquivImage hf B)

omit [DecidableEq Atom] in
theorem Theory.Equiv.bind_of_equiv_image {T : Theory Atom'} {f f' : Atom → Proposition Atom'}
    (hf : ∀ x : Atom, f x ≡[T] f' x) (A : Proposition Atom) : (A >>= f) ≡[T] A >>= f' := by
  constructor
  apply Theory.equiv.bindOfEquivImage (fun x => hf x |>.some)

instance : Congruence (Proposition Atom) T.Equiv where
  refl := equivalent_refl
  symm _ _ := equivalent_comm
  trans _ _ _ := equivalent_trans
  elim := by
    intro C A B e
    apply Theory.Equiv.bind_of_equiv_image
    rintro (none | x)
    · exact e
    · exact equivalent_refl (A := atom x)

the bind operation A >>= f is a substitution in A of f x : Proposition Atom' for each atom x in A, and Context.fill is substitution of a distinguished atom (and the identity on the others):

instance : HasContext (Proposition Atom) where
  Context := Proposition (Option Atom)
  fill c A := c >>= (Option.rec A pure)

the point is that preservation of equivalence by filling a context drops out as a special case of preservation of equivalence by substitution, which is proven by induction on the proposition (easier than induction on a one-hole context bc less cases) — the results Derivation.mapAndAnd & relatives are of independent interest (you need them for semantics anyway), and also easy to prove, eg

def Derivation.andAnd {A A' B B' : Proposition Atom} (DA : ⇓({A} ⊢[T] A')) (DB : ⇓({B} ⊢[T] B')) :
    ⇓({A ∧ B} ⊢[T] A' ∧ B') := by
  apply conjI
  · refine Derivation.cut (Γ := {A ∧ B}) (Δ := ∅) ?_ DA
    exact conjE₁ (B := B) <| ass <| by grind
  · refine Derivation.cut (Γ := {A ∧ B}) (Δ := ∅) ?_ DB
    exact conjE₂ (A := A) <| ass <| by grind

By "this" you are referring to the infamous expression problem, right? Since this concerns macros, you likely wanted to tag @Sebastian Ullrich, but while I'm here I can offer my thoughts, polished by Claude.

So, there are multiple ways to tackle the expression problem. I'll talk about 2.

W-types

W-types are the fixpoints of polynomial functors. In a discipline similar to https://github.com/alexkeizer/QpfTypes, one could derive for a given signature functor like

inductive Prop1F (Atom : Type u) (R : Type u) : Type u where
  | atom (x : Atom)
  | one
  | tensor (a b : R)

a decomposition into a polynomial functor (a type of shapes together with a family of positions, i.e. recursive occurrences, indexed over shapes):

inductive Prop1Shape (Atom : Type u) : Type u where
  | atom (x : Atom)
  | one
  | tensor

def Prop1Pos : Prop1Shape Atom → Type
  | .atom _ => Empty
  | .one    => Empty
  | .tensor => Bool

together with a bijection Prop1F Atom R ≅ Σ s : Prop1Shape Atom, Prop1Pos s → R. The fixpoint is then the W-type WType (Prop1Shape Atom) Prop1Pos, which is a first-class Lean inductive. Packing up everything neatly under the namespace Prop1 goes a long way towards first class inductive feeling.

Since polynomial functors are closed under coproduct (Sum on shapes, case-split on positions), extending with new constructors

inductive ExtraF (R : Type u) : Type u where
  | bot
  | parr (a b : R)

amounts to taking WType (Prop1Shape Atom ⊕ ExtraShape) (Sum.elim Prop1Pos ExtraPos), and the embedding from the smaller to the larger fixpoint is structural recursion wrapping shapes
with Sum.inl.

The translation from a signature functor to its polynomial decomposition, the bijection, fold/unfold theorems about the fixpoint, and the embedding between fixpoints are all purely mechanical and could be handled by a custom elaborator.

Object algebras

Object algebras are a much more lightweight encoding when you don't really need inductives and can define all relevant traversals by structural recursion. The idea is to represent each
group of constructors as a typeclass over a result type, and extend with extends:

class Prop1Syn (Atom : Type u) (repr : Type u) where
  atom : Atom → repr
  one : repr
  tensor : repr → repr → repr

class Prop2Syn (Atom : Type u) (repr : Type u) extends Prop1Syn Atom repr where
  bot : repr
  parr : repr → repr → repr

Generic definitions work over any repr with the right constructors:

def example1 [Prop1Syn Atom repr] (a b : Atom) : repr :=
  Prop1Syn.tensor (Prop1Syn.atom a) (Prop1Syn.atom b)

This formula is polymorphic in repr. It works at any current or future type that implements Prop1Syn. Each interpretation (evaluation, pretty-printing, translation) is just an instance:

instance : Prop1Syn Atom (Proposition1 Atom) where
  atom := .atom
  one := .one
  tensor := .tensor

instance : Prop1Syn Atom String where
  atom x := s!"<atom>"
  one := "1"
  tensor a b := s!"({a} ⊗ {b})"

The embedding from Prop1Syn into Prop2Syn is implicit: any function generic over [Prop1Syn Atom repr] automatically works wherever [Prop2Syn Atom repr] is available, since Prop2Syn extends Prop1Syn.

The tradeoff is that you cannot pattern-match on repr. You can only produce terms, not inspect them. If you need to consume propositions (e.g. decide equality, normalize), you need either a concrete inductive or a catamorphism added to the typeclass. In practice, many use cases (building terms, DSL embeddings, translations between languages) only need the production side.

fwiw i think the object algebra approach is the one taken by the formalised formal logic project, which works very cleanly. designing my corner of cslib i was conscious of the different aims here — if we just wanted a treatment of logic we should contribute to the extensive library that already exists right? that's why i landed on a much more explicit representation of derivations, bc in this context it plays very nicely (in fact arguably is up to naming hypotheses) STLC.

example [HasConj α] [HasConjIntro β] (Γ : γ) (A B : α) (D : Derivation (Γ ⊢ A)) (E : Derivation (Γ ⊢ B)) :
    Derivation (Γ ⊢ A ∧ B) := HasConjIntro.conjI D E

where α is the type of propositions and there's also some typeclass expressing that β is a type of derivations of α in context γ etc etc. the point is that you're applying a combinator HasConjIntro.conjI here, which is derivation-type agnostic
